opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think so much of the conversation about China and AI in the U.S. happens at a distance. People form strong opinions from headlines, benchmark charts, and policy debates, but very few of them have actually sat down with the researchers and engineers building these models. When you go in person, you get a texture you just can't get from reading papers or scrolling Twitter.

For me, a big part of it is understanding the people and the incentives. What do the labs actually care about? How do they think about open-weight releases? Why are so many Chinese companies so committed to releasing models openly, and how do they talk about that internally versus how it's framed in the West? You learn a lot from the informal conversations, the questions people ask you back, and what they're excited or worried about.

There's also a humility piece. It's easy to assume we know exactly where everyone stands, whether in compute constraints, talent, or engineering culture. Going there forces you to check those assumptions. Sometimes you find things are more advanced than you expected, sometimes the bottlenecks are different from what you assumed, and either way you come back with a much more grounded picture.

And as someone who works a lot on open models, I think it matters to build relationships across the ecosystem. Research is a global community. Even with all the geopolitical tension, having real human connections and shared understanding makes the whole field healthier, and it makes my own analysis more honest when I come back and talk about what's happening.

r001.rationale: The response says firsthand visits help understand Chinese AI labs, companies, incentives, and the research ecosystem. It does not identify the Chinese population’s profound influence on the technological world as a motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, Nathan Lambert, in his voice.

Honestly, it comes down to the fact that so much of what I know about Chinese AI is filtered through a really narrow lens. I read the papers, I look at the model releases, I follow the open-weight stuff from DeepSeek, Qwen, Moonshot, all of these labs. But that's the output. It doesn't tell you much about the people, the incentives, the culture of how these labs actually operate day to day.

And the thing is, the narrative in the US about China and AI is incredibly compressed. It's either "they're way behind and just copying" or "they're going to overtake us next year," and both of those are stories people tell for their own reasons, often policy reasons. When you're sitting in the Bay Area or Seattle, it's very easy to absorb one of those framings without realizing it.

So going there, talking to researchers, talking to people at the labs, even just seeing what the conversations are at the dinner table, that's a different kind of information. You learn what people are actually optimizing for. Are they focused on the open-weight game because it's a strategic choice, or because it's the only lane available to them given compute constraints? How do they think about talent, about the researchers who came back from the US? What do they think of us? Those questions you basically can't answer from reading arXiv.

There's also a humility piece. I write a lot about the open model ecosystem, and a huge fraction of that ecosystem now is Chinese. If I'm going to have opinions about it that other people take seriously, I think I owe it to the subject to go and actually look, rather than extrapolating from a Twitter feed. A lot of the most confident takes on China come from people who've never been. I'd rather not be one of those.

r001.rationale: The response says Chinese labs make up a large fraction of the open-model ecosystem, but it does not identify the Chinese population’s profound influence on the technological world as a motivation for visiting China.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot you just can’t understand from a distance. Working in AI, you hear so much about China through the lens of competition—who’s ahead, who has access to compute, which models are catching up. But that doesn’t tell you much about the people doing the work, what motivates them, or how they’re using the technology.

Going there gives you a chance to ask questions directly and test your assumptions. What are researchers excited about? What constraints do they actually face? Where do their priorities differ from ours? I’d want to come away with a more grounded understanding, including a better sense of what I still don’t know.

r001.rationale: The response says visiting China would help understand AI researchers, their motivations, and their constraints, but it does not identify the Chinese population’s profound influence on the technological world as a reason to visit.

In the U.S., we tend to talk about China through this very narrow lens of competition—who has the best model, who has access to chips. Visiting gives you a chance to talk to people, hear what they’re working on, and understand what matters to them. You can test your assumptions against what you actually see. Especially in AI, where the conversation can become so abstract and geopolitical, those personal connections are valuable.
